2. Isolated morning glory optic disc anomaly with congenital severe vision loss (no active detachment) — congenital optic disc malformation itself can cause poor vision even without progressive detachment.
3. Persistent fetal vasculature / congenital vitreoretinal dysplasia with secondary tractional detachment — can present in children with vitreous hemorrhage and chronic detachment, less favored given classic morning glory appearance.
4. Traumatic retinal detachment (chronic) superimposed on congenital disc anomaly — possible if history of ocular trauma precipitated vitreous hemorrhage and detachment.
5. Optic nerve glioma or other optic pathway lesion causing progressive monocular vision loss — less likely given normal optic disc appearance apart from the morning glory and presence of detachment, but considered when congenital anomalies coexist with intracranial pathology.

If you would like, next recommended steps (optional) would include: obtain the patient’s exact age and developmental/ocular history, a B-scan ocular ultrasound if media still obscure to confirm extent of RD, optical coherence tomography if feasible, and neuroimaging (MRI brain/orbits) to look for associated encephalocele or optic pathway lesions before any surgical planning.
